composition: Nominal composition Fe–18Mn–10Al–1.2C (wt%), i.e. Fe–18Mn–10Al–xC with x = 1.2 wt%. Measured chemical composition of the 1.2C heat (mass %): Al 10.19, Mn 17.45, C 1.16, Fe balance — Al and Mn are essentially constant across the series (Al 9.90–10.19, Mn 17.14–17.71) and only C was varied (0.48 → 0.77 → 1.16). In the Fe–Mn–Al–C system Mn and C are austenite stabilizers while Al is a ferrite stabilizer, so raising C to 1.2 wt% stabilizes a fully austenitic matrix while the heavy Al addition lowers density; the calculated density is 6.78 g/cm³ (calculation after Ref. 7) and the austenite stacking fault energy is estimated as 84.5 mJ/m² (model used previously, Ref. 13) — higher than the 73.4 and 77.9 mJ/m² of the 0.5C and 0.8C steels.
conclusions: Raising C from 0.5 to 1.2 wt% in Fe–18Mn–10Al–xC changes the as-quenched microstructure from a duplex ferritic–austenitic structure (with B2/DO3 ordered phases in ferrite and κ carbides in austenite at 0.8C) to a fully austenitic matrix with uniformly distributed κ carbides at 1.2C. This microstructural change gives the 1.2C steel the best strength–ductility combination of the series — UTS 946.7 MPa with 56.2% total elongation (UTS × TE = 53205 MPa·%, roughly twice that of the 0.5C steel) — and a pronounced, three-stage strain-hardening behaviour, versus two stages for the 0.5C and 0.8C steels. The paper's central methodological conclusion is that the Crussard–Jaoul analysis adequately describes the strain-hardening behaviour of duplex, complex and austenite-based low-density Fe–Mn–Al–C steels, and that at 1.2C it resolves a multistage hardening response directly traceable to the evolution of dislocation substructure (planar slip → Taylor lattice → microbands → microband interaction). This is the first reported C–J description of a high-stacking-fault-energy austenite-based alloy without a TWIP effect, and the results show that comparable or better strength–ductility can be achieved at lower Mn or C contents by controlled thermo-mechanical processing and heat treatment, which is useful input for alloy design of low-density automotive steels.
mechanisms: Carbon addition to 1.2 wt% fully stabilizes austenite and suppresses ferrite formation, so the as-quenched 1.2C steel is single-phase γ with κ carbides instead of the duplex structure of the lower-C steels.

The high Al + C alloying produces κ carbide [(Fe,Mn)3AlCx] precipitates (L'12 perovskite type) that are finely and uniformly distributed in the austenite matrix, and their high number density raises the yield strength of the 1.2C steel to 735.1 MPa despite its coarse grains (comparable to the finer-grained 0.8C steel).

Plastic deformation of the 1.2C austenite proceeds sequentially: planar slip at ε ≈ 0.02, a Taylor lattice-like dislocation arrangement by ε ≈ 0.07, well-developed microbands at ε ≈ 0.3, and microband–microband interaction at ε ≈ 0.4.

First (primary) hardening stage of the three-stage C–J behaviour (up to ε ≈ 0.026) is governed by the ease of planar slip in the austenite matrix, which explains the rapid initial decline in strain hardening rate.

Second (intermediate) stage, between ε ≈ 0.026 and ε ≈ 0.137, sustains the hardening rate because Taylor lattice and microband structures develop and keep the strain hardening high over a large strain range (plateau at ln(dσ/dε) ≈ 7.5).

Third (final) stage, beyond ε ≈ 0.137, shows a continuously rising hardening rate attributed to a further increase in microband density and the interaction/blocking of microbands in more than one direction.

Because the sustained multi-stage hardening delays strain localization to large strains, the 1.2C steel achieves markedly higher tensile ductility (56.2%) than the 0.5C and 0.8C steels, whose plasticity is exhausted before microband interaction can occur (hence no third stage and lower ductility).

The combination of a single austenitic matrix, high stacking fault energy (84.5 mJ/m²) and κ carbides means the alloy hardens by planar slip / microband mechanisms rather than by the TWIP twinning route typical of fully austenitic high-Mn steels.
microstructure: As-quenched 1.2C steel is fully austenitic (γ), with no ferrite, in contrast to the duplex ferritic–austenitic 0.5C and 0.8C steels (austenite fractions 59.2% and 84.8%, respectively). Optical microscopy (etched in 1 ml HCl + 100 ml methanol + 4 g picric acid) shows coarse equiaxed polygonal austenite grains containing abundant straight, parallel-sided annealing twins occurring as single or multiple sets. TEM (Tecnai G2 20, 200 kV; foils twinjet electropolished in 9% perchloric acid in methanol at −30 °C) shows fine κ carbide precipitates of the L'12 (perovskite) type, [(Fe,Mn)3AlCx], uniformly distributed in the austenite matrix; weak extra spots between the fundamental reflections appear in the SADP (indexed 131, 220, 110, 111) and a dark-field image of the γ phase shows a fine bright speckle throughout the field. The κ carbides are the only ordered phase present — the B2 [(Fe,Mn)Al] and DO3 [(Fe,Mn)3Al] domains found in the ferrite of the 0.8C steel are absent. Thus increasing C to 1.2 wt% converts the structure from duplex (with ordered phases in both constituents) to single-phase austenite plus κ carbides.
processing: Processing route (all steps belong to the as-quenched process chain): (1) 50 kg ingot of the 1.2C steel prepared by induction melting under an argon atmosphere; (2) forging at 1200 °C; (3) homogenization at 1200 °C for 3 h; (4) hot rolling at 1200 °C to 3.5 mm thickness with 90% reduction; (5) annealing of the hot-rolled strip at 1000 °C for 1 h; (6) cold rolling to 1 mm thickness; (7) final annealing/solution treatment at 1000 °C; (8) water quenching to room temperature, which defines the as-quenched terminal state studied here. No cooling rate or atmosphere is reported for the individual heat-treatment steps beyond the argon atmosphere used for melting.
properties: Room-temperature uniaxial tensile tests (universal testing machine SANSCMT5000, constant crosshead displacement velocity equivalent to an initial strain rate of 1.33×10⁻³ s⁻¹) give for the as-quenched 1.2C steel: yield strength 735.1 ± 5.0 MPa, ultimate tensile strength 946.7 ± 4.5 MPa, and total elongation 56.2 ± 1.0%. The product UTS × TE = 53205 MPa·%, almost twice that of the 0.5C steel (28100 MPa·%), and the highest of the three steels despite the 1.2C steel not having the highest UTS (the 0.8C steel peaks at 979.1 MPa). Calculated density is 6.78 g/cm³. The engineering stress–strain curve rises without a visible yield-point drop to a plateau near 940 MPa and extends to roughly 0.55–0.6 strain. Strain hardening rate (dσ/dε) versus true strain shows the 1.2C steel passing through a minimum near 1700 MPa and then holding a broad plateau near 1900 MPa before dropping to zero around 0.45 strain; C–J analysis (ln(dσ/dε) vs ln ε) resolves three hardening stages with breakpoints at ε = 0.026 and ε = 0.137 (steep first stage, flat plateau at roughly ln(dσ/dε) ≈ 7.5, then a rising third stage), whereas 0.5C and 0.8C steels show only two stages. The 1.2C steel sustains a sufficient strain hardening rate after 0.026 strain to prevent accumulation of large local strains. Characterization techniques applied to this sample: optical microscopy, TEM with selected-area diffraction (bright- and dark-field), uniaxial tensile testing, Crussard–Jaoul analysis of the flow curves, and TEM of interrupted tensile specimens at true strains 0.02, 0.07, 0.3 and 0.4.
summary: 1.2C steel is the highest-carbon member (nominally Fe–18Mn–10Al–1.2C, wt%) of a three-steel low-density Fe–18Mn–10Al–xC series (0.5, 0.8, 1.2 C wt%) in which carbon was the only deliberately varied element. A 50 kg induction-melted, forged, homogenized, hot-rolled, annealed, cold-rolled strip was given a final 1000 °C anneal followed by water quenching to room temperature, producing a fully austenitic microstructure with uniformly distributed κ carbides. The paper uses this sample, together with the 0.5C and 0.8C reference steels, to link initial microstructure to tensile behaviour and to strain-hardening stages analysed by the Crussard–Jaoul (C–J) method; the 1.2C steel is the only fully austenitic (ferrite-free) sample and the only one showing three-stage strain hardening.
unmapped: The 1.2C steel is the sample against which the paper benchmarks the series; its UTS × TE of 53205 MPa·% is described as almost twice that of the 0.5C steel (28100 MPa·%) and above the 0.8C steel (37597 MPa·%).

The paper notes that the existence of ordered phases in the 0.8C steel makes dislocation multiplication difficult (dominant single slip) and that κ carbides in austenite are reported to deteriorate strain hardening; the 1.2C steel nevertheless shows a rising third hardening stage, which the authors relate to its microband-dominated substructure.
Specific strength figures (e.g. 142.3 MPa·cm³/g) are reported in the paper only for the 0.8C steel, not for the 1.2C sample.
